## Charter

# CHARTER — Bridging the Interconnection Queue

## Deliverable
What: "Bridging the Interconnection Queue: State Policy Options for
Distributed Battery Storage, 2026-2030" — a policy research report.
Format: markdown, rendered last via the format skill (docx for state
legislative staff distribution).
Total size: 20000w

## Audience
State energy office policy directors and legislative committee staff who
already know what interconnection is but do not track battery-specific
queue data across states. They will skim the executive summary and read one
or two case studies closely; assume no prior exposure to Federal Order
2222-B.

## Voice & register
Third person, policy-analyst register — precise, unadorned, comfortable with
numbers. No first person, no rhetorical questions, no advocacy language;
present tradeoffs, not verdicts.

## Non-negotiables
1. Every statistic, dollar figure, or year carries a [S#] source tag traceable
   to a file in Sources of truth.
2. The terminology lock is followed exactly; no synonyms for locked terms.
3. Model legislation is always presented as an option among options, never as
   a recommendation the report insists a state adopt.
4. No section contains concluding or summarizing language except the
   Executive Summary and the Conclusion.
5. Case studies are presented as composites with tradeoffs stated, not as
   uncomplicated success stories.

## Terminology lock
- rooftop solar -> distributed solar
- battery storage -> battery energy storage system (BESS)
- utility -> distribution utility
- microgrid -> community microgrid
- ISO/RTO -> regional transmission organization (RTO)

## Sources of truth
- [S1] sources/ferc-order-2222-summary.md — summary memo, Federal Order 2222-B
- [S2] sources/state-survey-2026.md — 2026 eighteen-state interconnection survey
- [S3] sources/utility-interconnection-timelines.md — utility-reported queue data
- [S4] sources/case-studies-vermont-hawaii.md — two composite state case studies
- [S5] sources/cost-benefit-model-notes.md — cost-allocation modeling assumptions

## Acceptance criteria
1. Finished length is 20,000 words +/-20%.
2. Sections 3.1-3.3 describe interconnection queue mechanics consistent with
   [S1] and [S3]; no claim in those sections contradicts the source data.
3. Both case studies (4.1, 4.2) state at least one quantified tradeoff each,
   tagged [S4].
4. Section 5's cost-allocation comparison distinguishes observed data ([S2],
   [S3]) from illustrative modeling assumptions ([S5]) explicitly.
5. The Executive Summary is <=900 words and is comprehensible standing alone,
   without reading the rest of the report first.

## Out of scope
- Federal legislative process and any proposed changes to Federal Order
  2222-B itself.
- Wholesale electricity market design.
- Jurisdictions outside the United States.
- Net metering / retail rate design for exported energy (distinct policy
  question from interconnection queue processing).

rely on it. Later units read only the specific slices they need; this
catalog is the one place that summarizes all five in full.

## Sources

- [S1] sources/ferc-order-2222-summary.md — a regulatory-affairs summary
  memo describing Federal Order 2222-B and, specifically, what it does and
  does not change about retail interconnection authority. Feeds Section 2
  (Policy Landscape) and Section 3.3 (Technical Standards).

- [S2] sources/state-survey-2026.md — Cascadia Energy Policy Institute's
  2026 eighteen-state survey of battery energy storage system (BESS)

- [S3] sources/utility-interconnection-timelines.md — utility-reported

- [S4] sources/case-studies-vermont-hawaii.md — two composite state case
  studies (a shared-queue-priority program and a hosting-capacity-mapping
  program), each with quantified results and a stated tradeoff. Feeds

- [S5] sources/cost-benefit-model-notes.md — a methodology memo documenting
  illustrative cost-allocation modeling assumptions (applicant-pays,
  socialized-through-rates, hybrid threshold). Feeds Section 3.2 (Cost

## Cross-source cautions for downstream units

- [S1] is the only source that speaks to federal/state authority division —
  do not infer that division from [S2] or [S3], which are both retail-only
  queue data with no federal comparison.

- [S5]'s dollar figures ($180,000 per constraint, 40 applicants) are
  sensitivity-testing assumptions for Section 5.1's modeling and must never
  be presented as an observed cost in the report body.

- [S4]'s program-cost figures ($3.1M build, $410K/year, both from the
  shared-queue-priority case) are the only observed cost-allocation data in
  the source set; Section 5.2 should prefer these over [S5] wherever both
  could apply.

- [S2] and [S3] describe different populations (a multi-state survey vs.
  four named utilities) and should never be averaged together into a single
  headline figure; Section 3.1 should cite them as two distinct data points.

- [S4]'s two case studies are composites, not literal named states; Section
  4.1 and 4.2 should describe them as "a shared-savings queue reform" and
  "a hosting-capacity-mapping reform," never assert a specific real state.

### sources/ferc-order-2222-summary.md

# Summary memo — Federal Order 2222-B (fictional)

Prepared by Cascadia Energy Policy Institute, Regulatory Affairs Desk.

Federal Order 2222-B (issued 2024, effective for RTO/ISO compliance filings
through 2026) requires each regional transmission organization to accept
aggregations of distributed energy resources — rooftop solar, behind-the-meter
batteries, and controllable water heaters — as a single dispatchable resource
in wholesale markets, provided the aggregator can demonstrate telemetry at the
device level. [S1]

Three consequences matter for state interconnection policy:

1. The order does not touch retail interconnection rules. States retain full
   authority over how a distribution utility processes an interconnection
   application, the queue in which it sits, and who pays for upgrades the
   application triggers. Federal Order 2222-B only governs what happens once
   a resource is already interconnected and wants to sell into wholesale
   markets.
2. Utilities report that 2222-B compliance filings have pulled engineering
   staff away from retail interconnection review, lengthening queues by an
   estimated 15% in the twelve months after a utility's compliance filing is
   accepted, though this figure is self-reported and not independently
   audited.
3. Aggregators now have a federal hook to demand faster retail
   interconnection, since a resource stuck in a retail queue cannot
   participate in the wholesale aggregation the order enables. This creates
   pressure states did not anticipate when 2222-B was issued.

Nothing in this memo should be read as a claim about wholesale market design;
that is out of scope for this report.
